title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
constraints: nums may contain negative numbers, so the plain sliding window does not work

examples.explanation: The subarrays [1,1] at index 0 and [1,1] at index 1 both sum to 2.
The subarray [1,2] and the single element [3] both sum to 3.

hints.content: A sliding window cannot work here because the array contains negative numbers. What can you do instead of adjusting the window boundaries?
Turn every subarray into a subtraction of two prefix sums.
sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1]. If the running sum is s, how many earlier running sums must have been equal to s - k?

Map<running sum, count of times seen>
start with {0: 1} so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted
for each number:
    running += number
    answer += map.getOrDefault(running - k, 0)
    map.merge(running, 1, Integer::sum)
Use HashMap<Integer, Integer> counts. It must be seeded with {0 -> 1}, otherwise every subarray that starts at index 0 is missed.

invariant: counts holds the number of times each running prefix sum has appeared so far, including the empty prefix 0.
whyThisPattern: The signal is 'contiguous range' but the array can contain negative numbers, so the window cannot be steered by growing and shrinking. Prefix sums replace the range with a subtraction, and the subtraction becomes a HashMap lookup, which is exactly the hashing pattern.
bruteForce: Compute the sum of every subarray: for i, extend j and accumulate. That is O(n^2) time. At n = 10,000 it is about 5 * 10^7 additions, which is already too slow for repeated calls. With prefix sums and a frequency map each element is processed once, so the same work becomes O(n).
interviewExplanation: I keep a running prefix sum and a map from each prefix sum to how many times it has appeared. For a subarray ending at the current index to sum to k, the prefix before it must equal running minus k, so I add how many times that value was seen. I seed the map with zero so subarrays that start at index 0 are counted, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to seed the map with {0: 1}, which drops every subarray starting at index 0.
Adding the count to the answer before incrementing the current running sum, which would allow an empty subarray.
Assuming the sliding window trick works even though negative values break monotonicity.

animationSteps.title: The window trick is blocked
animationSteps.description: Negative values mean shrinking the window can make the sum go up.
animationSteps.text: Because the array contains negative numbers, expanding and shrinking a window cannot reliably control the sum.

animationSteps.title: Rewrite the range as a subtraction
animationSteps.description: Any subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums.
animationSteps.text: The subarray sum from index i to j equals prefix at j plus one minus prefix at i.

animationSteps.title: Predict the move
animationSteps.description: The running sum is s. Which earlier running sum do we need to count?
animationSteps.text: Given the running sum s, choose the earlier running sum that completes a subarray summing to k.

payload.prompt: running sum = 1, k = 0. Which earlier prefix sum forms a subarray that sums to k?
payload.explanation: running - k = 1 - 0 = 1, which has appeared once already

animationSteps.title: Counts of running sums
animationSteps.description: Start with the empty prefix so index 0 is counted.
animationSteps.text: The map starts with prefix sum 0 appearing once, which represents the empty prefix.

animationSteps.title: First element
animationSteps.text: After adding 1 the running sum is 1. Looking for 1 minus 0 which is 1, and 1 has not appeared yet.

animationSteps.title: Second element
animationSteps.description: running becomes 0, look for 0 - 0 = 0, seen once.
animationSteps.text: After adding -1 the running sum is 0. Looking for 0 minus 0 which is 0, seen once, so one subarray is counted.

animationSteps.title: Two distinct subarrays, same sum
animationSteps.description: Running sum 0 has now been seen twice, which is why counts must be stored, not just seen.
animationSteps.text: The map now holds prefix 0 twice and prefix 1 once. Storing counts rather than booleans is what makes the counting correct.

animationSteps.title: Counted in one pass
animationSteps.description: Each element produced at most one map lookup.
animationSteps.text: The whole count is produced by one pass with one lookup and one update per element.

payload.message: Every subarray was found with a single pass, no nested loops.
